rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 0° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 2.82 cal.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail. Use a longer rail or a higher-thrust motor.
Below the usual 5:1 minimum. Choose a higher-thrust motor or lighten the rocket.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Slow off the rail: 47 ft/s with an average thrust-to-weight of 3.7:1. Use a longer rail or a higher-thrust motor.
Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 0° from vertical)
Chute opens 1.2 s after apogee at 28 ft/s
Average thrust-to-weight is 3.7:1, below the usual 5:1 minimum
example-0|calm.mdnote: The charge fires 3 s after burnout. The A8 is sold with 0, 3, 5 s delays.

example-0|calm.report: Opened Big Bertha.DetailsOpened Big Bertha. Weight without motor 0.16 lb, CG 11.3 in, length 21.1 in. Motor set to A8. Free-form fins keep their exact shape from the file; drag and stability are calculated from that shape.Weight, CG and turning inertia are computed from the file’s components and materials. If you have weighed and balanced the real rocket, select the stage in the design tree and enter your numbers there.
guide: No lugs or buttons needed in a tower; the fins must clear its rails.
The launch lug is too small for a 1/8 in rod: its inside diameter, 0.113 in, needs to be at least 0.137 in.
The launch lug is set for a 1/8 in rod, not a 3/16 in rod. Use the matching rod, or change the lug's type.
The launch lug is set for a 1/8 in rod, not a 1/4 in rod. Use the matching rod, or change the lug's type.
The rocket has a rod-type launch lug but no rail buttons or rail-type lug, so it can't fly from a rail. Use a rod, or add rail buttons or a rail-type lug.
The rocket has a rod-type launch lug but no rail buttons or rail-type lug, so it can't fly from a rail. Use a rod, or add rail buttons or a rail-type lug.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 21° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.71 cal.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail. Use a longer rail or a higher-thrust motor.
Below the usual 5:1 minimum. Choose a higher-thrust motor or lighten the rocket.
Leaves the cone while the motor burns. Wait for less wind, reduce the rail angle, or use a faster motor or longer rail.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Slow off the rail: 45 ft/s with an average thrust-to-weight of 3.7:1. Use a longer rail or a higher-thrust motor.
Strong weathercocking: the crosswind meets the rocket at up to 21° just after it leaves the rail, and it is 34° from vertical at burnout. Use a longer rail or a faster motor, or wait for less wind.

Leaves the 20° safety cone under power: 35° from vertical while the motor is still burning. A low, fast flight path can reach spectators or the parking area. Wait for less wind, use a faster motor or longer rail, or reduce the rail angle.
Chute opens 1.3 s after apogee at 46 ft/s

example-0|delay=null.report: Opened Big Bertha.DetailsOpened Big Bertha. Weight without motor 0.16 lb, CG 11.3 in, length 21.1 in. Motor set to A8. Free-form fins keep their exact shape from the file; drag and stability are calculated from that shape.Weight, CG and turning inertia are computed from the file’s components and materials. If you have weighed and balanced the real rocket, select the stage in the design tree and enter your numbers there.
guide: No lugs or buttons needed in a tower; the fins must clear its rails.
The launch lug is too small for a 1/8 in rod: its inside diameter, 0.113 in, needs to be at least 0.137 in.
The launch lug is set for a 1/8 in rod, not a 3/16 in rod. Use the matching rod, or change the lug's type.
The launch lug is set for a 1/8 in rod, not a 1/4 in rod. Use the matching rod, or change the lug's type.
The rocket has a rod-type launch lug but no rail buttons or rail-type lug, so it can't fly from a rail. Use a rod, or add rail buttons or a rail-type lug.
The rocket has a rod-type launch lug but no rail buttons or rail-type lug, so it can't fly from a rail. Use a rod, or add rail buttons or a rail-type lug.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 9° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.51 cal.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
Below the usual 5:1 minimum. Choose a higher-thrust motor or lighten the rocket.
Leaves the cone while the motor burns. Wait for less wind, reduce the rail angle, or use a faster motor or longer rail.
Fires 1.8 s before apogee. Drill or choose a delay closer to the ideal.
Opens fast: risk of zippering or a broken shock cord. Set deployment closer to apogee.
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Leaves the 20° safety cone under power: 62° from vertical while the motor is still burning. A low, fast flight path can reach spectators or the parking area. Wait for less wind, use a faster motor or longer rail, or reduce the rail angle.
Chute opens 1.8 s before apogee, at 138 ft/s. Use a delay closer to the ideal motor delay for apogee.
Average thrust-to-weight is 2.1:1, below the usual 5:1 minimum

example-0|delay=9.5.report: Opened Big Bertha.DetailsOpened Big Bertha. Weight without motor 0.16 lb, CG 11.3 in, length 21.1 in. Motor set to A8. Free-form fins keep their exact shape from the file; drag and stability are calculated from that shape.Weight, CG and turning inertia are computed from the file’s components and materials. If you have weighed and balanced the real rocket, select the stage in the design tree and enter your numbers there.
guide: No lugs or buttons needed in a tower; the fins must clear its rails.
The launch lug is too small for a 1/8 in rod: its inside diameter, 0.113 in, needs to be at least 0.137 in.
The launch lug is set for a 1/8 in rod, not a 3/16 in rod. Use the matching rod, or change the lug's type.
The launch lug is set for a 1/8 in rod, not a 1/4 in rod. Use the matching rod, or change the lug's type.
The rocket has a rod-type launch lug but no rail buttons or rail-type lug, so it can't fly from a rail. Use a rod, or add rail buttons or a rail-type lug.
The rocket has a rod-type launch lug but no rail buttons or rail-type lug, so it can't fly from a rail. Use a rod, or add rail buttons or a rail-type lug.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 9° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.51 cal.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
Below the usual 5:1 minimum. Choose a higher-thrust motor or lighten the rocket.
Leaves the cone while the motor burns. Wait for less wind, reduce the rail angle, or use a faster motor or longer rail.
Fires 7.7 s after apogee. Drill or choose a delay closer to the ideal.
Opens fast: risk of zippering or a broken shock cord. Set deployment closer to apogee.
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
A hard opening. Check the shock cord, harness and anchors.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Leaves the 20° safety cone under power: 62° from vertical while the motor is still burning. A low, fast flight path can reach spectators or the parking area. Wait for less wind, use a faster motor or longer rail, or reduce the rail angle.
Chute opens 7.8 s after apogee, at 132 ft/s and 640 ft below apogee. Use a delay closer to the ideal motor delay for apogee.
Average thrust-to-weight is 2.1:1, below the usual 5:1 minimum
Hard parachute opening: about 7 lbf (34 g on the airframe) as it fills at 132 ft/s. Check the shock cord, quick links and anchors are rated well above this, or open it at a lower speed.
example-0|reopen.mdnote: The charge fires 9.5 s after burnout. The D2 is sold with 0 s delays or plugged; reload delays can be drilled shorter.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 0° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.91 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 0.0972 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Below 1 caliber. Add 0.1447 lb of nose weight at mid-nose or larger fins before flying.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

This flight goes supersonic, where stability estimates are less certain than below Mach 1. In NASA wind-tunnel tests of a long, slender sounding rocket, the center of pressure moved forward by about 7% of the body length for a moment near Mach 1, which this app doesn't model; a shorter version of the same rocket showed no dip. Fins with square edges are counted cautiously (less fin lift) above Mach 1, so the real margin there is probably a little higher. Leave extra margin, confirm the fins are built as designed, and discuss the flight with your RSO.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 3.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 4.1 s after apogee. Drill or choose a delay closer to the ideal.
Opens while still moving; check the shock cord and attachment points.
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Transonic or supersonic: estimates are less certain, and fins, nose and joints take higher loads.
Peak airspeed is 226% of the estimated flutter speed (501 ft/s), so the fins could flutter and fail. Thicker or stiffer fins, or tip-to-tip reinforcement, raise it.
flags: Unstable or near-unstable (0.85 cal). Add nose weight.
Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 1° from vertical)
Chute opens 4.1 s after apogee, at 51 ft/s and 156 ft below apogee. Use a delay closer to the ideal motor delay for apogee.
Transonic flight. Drag estimate is less reliable above Mach 0.8.

Fin flutter likely: at T+1.7 s the airspeed is 226% of the estimated flutter speed (501 ft/s at 1,122 ft), for fins of Aircraft plywood (LOC) (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.
Descent is fast (25 ft/s). Consider a larger parachute.
example-1|calm.mdnote: The charge fires 14 s after burnout. The K550 is sold with 0, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 18 s delays; reload delays can be drilled shorter.

This flight goes supersonic, where stability estimates are less certain than below Mach 1. In NASA wind-tunnel tests of a long, slender sounding rocket, the center of pressure moved forward by about 7% of the body length for a moment near Mach 1, which this app doesn't model; a shorter version of the same rocket showed no dip. Fins with square edges are counted cautiously (less fin lift) above Mach 1, so the real margin there is probably a little higher. Leave extra margin, confirm the fins are built as designed, and discuss the flight with your RSO.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 5° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.93 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 0.0844 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight. The CP estimate is good to about ±0.2 cal on this rocket, so it could be below 1.
Stability as a share of length

1.04 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.0063 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

This flight goes supersonic, where stability estimates are less certain than below Mach 1. In NASA wind-tunnel tests of a long, slender sounding rocket, the center of pressure moved forward by about 7% of the body length for a moment near Mach 1, which this app doesn't model; a shorter version of the same rocket showed no dip. Fins with square edges are counted cautiously (less fin lift) above Mach 1, so the real margin there is probably a little higher. Leave extra margin, confirm the fins are built as designed, and discuss the flight with your RSO.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 3.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
The chute is set to open at the motor ejection charge, but the motor is plugged: nothing opens and the rocket comes down ballistic.
Transonic or supersonic: estimates are less certain, and fins, nose and joints take higher loads.
Peak airspeed is 273% of the estimated flutter speed (501 ft/s), so the fins could flutter and fail. Thicker or stiffer fins, or tip-to-tip reinforcement, raise it.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 7° from vertical)
The chute is set to open at the motor ejection charge, but the motor is plugged (Motor tab, Motor Delay): nothing opens and the rocket comes down ballistic.
Transonic flight. Drag estimate is less reliable above Mach 0.8.

Aerodynamic heating: the air stopped at the nose tip reaches about 210 °F at Mach 1.2. Many laminating epoxies soften around 60–120 °C (140–250 °F); the nose tip and fin leading edges heat first. How hot the parts actually get depends on how long the rocket stays fast.
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.93 cal at 5° to the airflow in this wind.

Fin flutter likely: at T+1.3 s the airspeed is 273% of the estimated flutter speed (501 ft/s at 1,125 ft), for fins of Aircraft plywood (LOC) (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.
Descent is fast (28 ft/s). Consider a larger parachute.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 5° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.93 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 0.0844 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight. The CP estimate is good to about ±0.2 cal on this rocket, so it could be below 1.
Stability as a share of length

1.04 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.0063 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

This flight goes supersonic, where stability estimates are less certain than below Mach 1. In NASA wind-tunnel tests of a long, slender sounding rocket, the center of pressure moved forward by about 7% of the body length for a moment near Mach 1, which this app doesn't model; a shorter version of the same rocket showed no dip. Fins with square edges are counted cautiously (less fin lift) above Mach 1, so the real margin there is probably a little higher. Leave extra margin, confirm the fins are built as designed, and discuss the flight with your RSO.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 3.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 11.2 s before apogee. Drill or choose a delay closer to the ideal.
Opens fast: risk of zippering or a broken shock cord. Set deployment closer to apogee.
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Transonic or supersonic: estimates are less certain, and fins, nose and joints take higher loads.
Peak airspeed is 273% of the estimated flutter speed (501 ft/s), so the fins could flutter and fail. Thicker or stiffer fins, or tip-to-tip reinforcement, raise it.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 7° from vertical)
Chute opens 11.2 s before apogee, at 1,097 ft/s. Use a delay closer to the ideal motor delay for apogee.
Transonic flight. Drag estimate is less reliable above Mach 0.8.

Aerodynamic heating: the air stopped at the nose tip reaches about 210 °F at Mach 1.2. Many laminating epoxies soften around 60–120 °C (140–250 °F); the nose tip and fin leading edges heat first. How hot the parts actually get depends on how long the rocket stays fast.
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.93 cal at 5° to the airflow in this wind.

Fin flutter likely: at T+1.3 s the airspeed is 273% of the estimated flutter speed (501 ft/s at 1,125 ft), for fins of Aircraft plywood (LOC) (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.
Descent is fast (28 ft/s). Consider a larger parachute.

example-1|delay=4.label: example-1|delay=4
rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 5° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.93 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 0.0844 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight. The CP estimate is good to about ±0.2 cal on this rocket, so it could be below 1.
Stability as a share of length

1.04 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.0063 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

This flight goes supersonic, where stability estimates are less certain than below Mach 1. In NASA wind-tunnel tests of a long, slender sounding rocket, the center of pressure moved forward by about 7% of the body length for a moment near Mach 1, which this app doesn't model; a shorter version of the same rocket showed no dip. Fins with square edges are counted cautiously (less fin lift) above Mach 1, so the real margin there is probably a little higher. Leave extra margin, confirm the fins are built as designed, and discuss the flight with your RSO.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 3.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 7.2 s before apogee. Drill or choose a delay closer to the ideal.
Opens fast: risk of zippering or a broken shock cord. Set deployment closer to apogee.
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Transonic or supersonic: estimates are less certain, and fins, nose and joints take higher loads.
Peak airspeed is 273% of the estimated flutter speed (501 ft/s), so the fins could flutter and fail. Thicker or stiffer fins, or tip-to-tip reinforcement, raise it.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 7° from vertical)
Chute opens 7.2 s before apogee, at 311 ft/s. Use a delay closer to the ideal motor delay for apogee.
Transonic flight. Drag estimate is less reliable above Mach 0.8.

Aerodynamic heating: the air stopped at the nose tip reaches about 210 °F at Mach 1.2. Many laminating epoxies soften around 60–120 °C (140–250 °F); the nose tip and fin leading edges heat first. How hot the parts actually get depends on how long the rocket stays fast.
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.93 cal at 5° to the airflow in this wind.

Fin flutter likely: at T+1.3 s the airspeed is 273% of the estimated flutter speed (501 ft/s at 1,125 ft), for fins of Aircraft plywood (LOC) (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.
Descent is fast (28 ft/s). Consider a larger parachute.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 5° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.93 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 0.0844 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight. The CP estimate is good to about ±0.2 cal on this rocket, so it could be below 1.
Stability as a share of length

1.04 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.0063 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

This flight goes supersonic, where stability estimates are less certain than below Mach 1. In NASA wind-tunnel tests of a long, slender sounding rocket, the center of pressure moved forward by about 7% of the body length for a moment near Mach 1, which this app doesn't model; a shorter version of the same rocket showed no dip. Fins with square edges are counted cautiously (less fin lift) above Mach 1, so the real margin there is probably a little higher. Leave extra margin, confirm the fins are built as designed, and discuss the flight with your RSO.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 3.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 1.7 s before apogee. Drill or choose a delay closer to the ideal.
Opens while still moving; check the shock cord and attachment points.
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Transonic or supersonic: estimates are less certain, and fins, nose and joints take higher loads.
Peak airspeed is 273% of the estimated flutter speed (501 ft/s), so the fins could flutter and fail. Thicker or stiffer fins, or tip-to-tip reinforcement, raise it.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 7° from vertical)
Chute opens 1.7 s before apogee, at 62 ft/s. Use a delay closer to the ideal motor delay for apogee.
Transonic flight. Drag estimate is less reliable above Mach 0.8.

Aerodynamic heating: the air stopped at the nose tip reaches about 210 °F at Mach 1.2. Many laminating epoxies soften around 60–120 °C (140–250 °F); the nose tip and fin leading edges heat first. How hot the parts actually get depends on how long the rocket stays fast.
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.93 cal at 5° to the airflow in this wind.

Fin flutter likely: at T+1.3 s the airspeed is 273% of the estimated flutter speed (501 ft/s at 1,125 ft), for fins of Aircraft plywood (LOC) (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.
Descent is fast (28 ft/s). Consider a larger parachute.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 0° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.80 cal.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length

1.52 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.0286 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 12.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
A little fast; 15–20 ft/s (4.5–6 m/s) is the usual target. A larger chute helps.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 1° from vertical)
The H148 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.

example-2|wind.label: example-2|wind
rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 16° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.45 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 0.4754 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length

1.52 cal is only 10% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.0286 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 12.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Leaves the cone while the motor burns. Wait for less wind, reduce the rail angle, or use a faster motor or longer rail.
Opens while still moving; check the shock cord and attachment points.
A little fast; 15–20 ft/s (4.5–6 m/s) is the usual target. A larger chute helps.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Noticeable weathercocking: up to 16° angle of attack off the rail, and it is 19° from vertical at burnout.

Leaves the 20° safety cone under power: 21° from vertical while the motor is still burning. A low, fast flight path can reach spectators or the parking area. Wait for less wind, use a faster motor or longer rail, or reduce the rail angle.
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.45 cal at 16° to the airflow in this wind.
The H148 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.
example-2|wind.mdnote: Plugged: no ejection charge fires. The H148 is sold with 0, 4, 6, 8, 10, 11, 14 s delays; reload delays can be drilled shorter.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 5° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.84 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 0.1871 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight. The CP estimate is good to about ±0.4 cal on this rocket, so it could be below 1.
Stability as a share of length

1.17 cal is only 7% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.3081 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 12.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
A little fast; 15–20 ft/s (4.5–6 m/s) is the usual target. A larger chute helps.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 7° from vertical)
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.84 cal at 5° to the airflow in this wind.
The J420 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.
example-2|delay=null.mdnote: Plugged: no ejection charge fires. The J420 is sold with 0, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14 s delays; reload delays can be drilled shorter.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 5° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 0.84 cal. A longer rail, a faster motor, nose weight or less wind raises it. 1 cal here takes 0.1871 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight. The CP estimate is good to about ±0.4 cal on this rocket, so it could be below 1.
Stability as a share of length

1.17 cal is only 7% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.3081 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 12.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 2.7 s before apogee. With an altimeter doing deployment, use a plugged motor or a delay as backup set near the ideal.

The motor’s ejection charge fires 2.7 s before apogee (3,477 ft, 95 ft/s) while the parachute is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
A little fast; 15–20 ft/s (4.5–6 m/s) is the usual target. A larger chute helps.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 7° from vertical)

The motor’s ejection charge fires 2.7 s before apogee (3,477 ft, 95 ft/s) while the parachute is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Stability leaving the rail drops to 0.84 cal at 5° to the airflow in this wind.
The J420 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.
example-2|reopen.mdnote: The charge fires 9.5 s after burnout. The J420 is sold with 0, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14 s delays; reload delays can be drilled shorter.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.82 cal.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
Typical drogue rates are 50–100 ft/s (15–30 m/s).
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 8° from vertical)
Main descent is fast (24 ft/s). Consider a larger main.
The J420 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.
example-3|motors.mdnote: Plugged: no ejection charge fires. The J420 is sold with 0, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14 s delays; reload delays can be drilled shorter.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.82 cal.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 8.1 s before apogee. With an altimeter doing deployment, use a plugged motor or a delay as backup set near the ideal.

The motor’s ejection charge fires 8.1 s before apogee (2,385 ft, 317 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
Typical drogue rates are 50–100 ft/s (15–30 m/s).
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 8° from vertical)

The motor’s ejection charge fires 8.1 s before apogee (2,385 ft, 317 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Main descent is fast (24 ft/s). Consider a larger main.
The J420 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.
example-3|delay=4.mdnote: The charge fires 4 s after burnout. The J420 is sold with 0, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14 s delays; reload delays can be drilled shorter.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.82 cal.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 2.6 s before apogee. With an altimeter doing deployment, use a plugged motor or a delay as backup set near the ideal.

The motor’s ejection charge fires 2.6 s before apogee (3,425 ft, 98 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
Typical drogue rates are 50–100 ft/s (15–30 m/s).
Too fast for a safe landing. Use a larger parachute.
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 8° from vertical)

The motor’s ejection charge fires 2.6 s before apogee (3,425 ft, 98 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Main descent is fast (24 ft/s). Consider a larger main.
The J420 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.

Free-form fins keep their exact shape from the file; drag and stability are calculated from that shape.Used the stage weight and CG override from the file.Weight, CG and turning inertia are computed from the file’s components and materials. If you have weighed and balanced the real rocket, select the stage in the design tree and enter your numbers there.
guide: No lugs or buttons needed in a tower; the fins must clear its rails.
The rocket has rail-type launch lugs but no rod-type launch lug, so it can't fly from a rod. Use a rail, or add a rod-type lug.

1010 rail-type launch lugs match the rail.

example-4|wind.label: example-4|wind
rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 12° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.11 cal.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Opens fast: risk of zippering or a broken shock cord. Set deployment closer to apogee.
Typical drogue rates are 50–100 ft/s (15–30 m/s).
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Noticeable weathercocking: up to 11° angle of attack off the rail, and it is 16° from vertical at burnout.
Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 16° from vertical)
The I300 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.
example-4|wind.mdnote: Plugged: no ejection charge fires. The I300 is sold with 4, 6, 8, 10, 14 s delays; reload delays can be drilled shorter.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 6° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.18 cal.
Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight.
Stability as a share of length

1.47 cal is only 9% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.0933 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 6° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.18 cal.
Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight.
Stability as a share of length

1.47 cal is only 9% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.0933 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 14.5 s before apogee. With an altimeter doing deployment, use a plugged motor or a delay as backup set near the ideal.

The motor’s ejection charge fires 14.5 s before apogee (684 ft, 707 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Opens while still moving; check the shock cord and attachment points.
Typical drogue rates are 50–100 ft/s (15–30 m/s).
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 8° from vertical)

The motor’s ejection charge fires 14.5 s before apogee (684 ft, 707 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
The J420 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 6° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.18 cal.
Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight.
Stability as a share of length

1.47 cal is only 9% of this rocket's length. Long, thin rockets lose margin quickly when they tilt; 10–15% of the length is a common guide for them. Reaching 10% takes 0.0933 lb of nose weight at mid-nose.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 7.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Fires 10.5 s before apogee. With an altimeter doing deployment, use a plugged motor or a delay as backup set near the ideal.

The motor’s ejection charge fires 10.5 s before apogee (2,840 ft, 412 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
Opens while still moving; check the shock cord and attachment points.
Typical drogue rates are 50–100 ft/s (15–30 m/s).
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 8° from vertical)

The motor’s ejection charge fires 10.5 s before apogee (2,840 ft, 412 ft/s) while the drogue is still packed. The simulation opens it as the design sets it, but a live charge can blow it out early or damage the rocket. Use a plugged motor if an altimeter handles deployment, or set the chute to open at the motor ejection charge with a delay near the ideal.
The J420 (38 mm) is smaller than the 54 mm motor mount. Fly it with a 38-to-54 mm motor adapter.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.82 cal.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 8.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 6° from vertical)

Fin flutter likely: at T+1.3 s the airspeed is 116% of the estimated flutter speed (474 ft/s at 403 ft), for fins of Birch plywood (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.

rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 7° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.87 cal.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 8.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 6° from vertical)

This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.

builder|cluster.label: builder|cluster
rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 5° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.27 cal.
Just above the 1 caliber minimum. Confirm the CG with the motor in, and consider a little nose weight.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 8.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Transonic or supersonic: estimates are less certain, and fins, nose and joints take higher loads.
Above Mach 0.8 from T+1.2 to T+1.5 s. Set the barometric altimeter's Mach (or apogee) lockout so the pressure jump can't fire a charge early.
Peak airspeed is 195% of the estimated flutter speed (476 ft/s), so the fins could flutter and fail. Thicker or stiffer fins, or tip-to-tip reinforcement, raise it.
Clustered rockets need larger distances from the pad than single-motor rockets of the same total impulse, and are usually flown heads-up.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 4° from vertical)
Transonic flight. Drag estimate is less reliable above Mach 0.8.

Barometric altimeters can be fooled by the pressure jump near Mach 1 and fire a charge early. The rocket is above Mach 0.8 from T+1.2 to T+1.5 s; set the altimeter’s Mach lockout (or apogee lockout) to at least 3 s after liftoff.

Fin flutter likely: at T+1.3 s the airspeed is 195% of the estimated flutter speed (476 ft/s at 671 ft), for fins of Birch plywood (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.

builder|three-stage.label: builder|three-stage
rso: In this wind the airflow meets the rocket at 8° as it leaves the rail. Body lift moves the CP forward as it tilts, leaving 1.79 cal.
At least 1 caliber is the usual minimum; this has margin.
Stability as a share of length
The CP is at least 10% of the rocket's length behind the CG, a common guide for long rockets.
Within the usual 0.05–0.3: gusts die out in a few swings.

Added up from the parts list, not weighed. Built rockets usually come out heavier, which lowers apogee and moves the CG. Weigh the rocket ready to fly without its motor, find its balance point, and enter both on the Rocket tab (select the stage in the design tree).
Guideline at least 50 ft/s, on a 8.0 ft rail.
At least 5:1 is the usual minimum.
Stays inside the cone while the motor burns.
Slow, near apogee: a gentle opening.
At or below about 20 ft/s (6 m/s).
Subsonic: the drag estimate is most reliable here.
Peak airspeed is 179% of the estimated flutter speed (485 ft/s), so the fins could flutter and fail. Thicker or stiffer fins, or tip-to-tip reinforcement, raise it.
Staged rockets need larger distances from the pad than single-motor rockets of the same total impulse, and are usually flown heads-up.
flags: Stays inside the 20° safety cone under power (up to 7° from vertical)

Fin flutter likely: at T+3.8 s the airspeed is 179% of the estimated flutter speed (485 ft/s at 1,963 ft), for fins of Birch plywood (shear modulus about 0.6 GPa). This is a rough, conservative estimate; thicker fins, a stiffer material, a smaller span or tip-to-tip reinforcement raise the flutter speed.
